subtype: Beckoning and thumbs-up copied from adults [Expressing]
passage: On the bus in Toronto, Tariq, two, sat on his caregiver Rosa's lap and curled his finger towards a pigeon on the window ledge, “Come, come.” The pigeon stayed put. Then the driver called “Ready?” and Tariq put up a thumb, copying Rosa. The driver gave a thumb back and grinned. Tariq looked at his own thumb, delighted, and did it again to a woman across the aisle. She lifted a thumb too. Rosa laughed. He did not know what it meant, only what it made happen.

qa.q: Who did Tariq beckon at the bus window?
qa.a: A pigeon on the window ledge.

qa.q: What does Tariq's delighted look at his thumb suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he enjoys the response he gets more than knowing the meaning of the gesture. He might also just like copying Rosa.

qa.q: What could Rosa do to help Tariq understand these gestures?
qa.a: Rosa could say “good” or “come here” as she gestures so that words and movements go together.

qa.q: How might the woman across the aisle feel about the thumb?
qa.a: She may feel touched or amused by a child's friendly gesture and enjoy returning it.

grounding: A toddler copies beckoning and thumbs-up gestures from adults without full understanding, and the meaning follows the response he sees.

passage: From the vegetable stall I watched Tenzin, two, on his grandmother Nirmala's hip. He curled his finger in the air towards a passing cow, “Come,” though the cow ignored him. When Nirmala bought him a biscuit, he raised his thumb high because she did, and grinned. The vendor gave him a thumb back. I don't think Tenzin knows what it means yet, but the reaction made him do it again. Nirmala looked at me, laughing. “He copies everything.”

qa.q: What did Tenzin do towards the passing cow?
qa.a: He curled his finger in the air and said “Come”.

qa.q: What does the narrator think Tenzin understands about the thumb?
qa.a: The narrator thinks he does not know the meaning yet, but repeats it because people react warmly. That is only the narrator's impression.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do to build on the gesture?
qa.a: She could say “good, thank you” with the thumb so the gesture and words go together.

qa.q: How might the vendor feel when Tenzin gives him a thumbs-up?
qa.a: The vendor may feel amused and pleased that a small child treats him as a friend.

grounding: A toddler copies come-here and thumbs-up gestures from adults, and the narrator sees that the meaning follows the reaction.

passage:
Monday: Noor, the daycare teacher, gave the children a thumbs-up after tidying. Dhruv stuck his thumb up too, and kept doing it all day, even when he spilled his milk.
Wednesday: whenever Dhruv's thumb went up, Noor said, "Yay!" and smiled.
The next Tuesday: Dhruv finished his banana, looked straight at Noor and held his thumb up high, waiting for her smile.

qa.q: When did Dhruv first copy the thumbs-up?
qa.a: On Monday, after Noor gave the children a thumbs-up after tidying.

qa.q: What did Dhruv seem to want by the next Tuesday when he held his thumb up?
qa.a: He seemed to want Noor's smile and approval, feeling proud of finishing his banana; the gesture had begun to mean "I did it".

qa.q: What made the thumbs-up start to mean something for Dhruv?
qa.a: Noor's steady "Yay!" and smile each time, which linked the gesture to a happy response.

qa.q: How might Noor see the thumbs-up after the spilled milk on Monday?
qa.a: Noor probably found it funny, knowing Dhruv was copying the shape without knowing what it meant yet.

grounding: Over several days a toddler copies a thumbs-up, and its meaning grows from the response he sees.

subtype: Beckoning and thumbs-up copied from adults [Expressing]
passage:
In the Chennai flat, Yamini curled her fingers at the cat. "Come, come, Pinky." The cat came.
Manjula, sitting on the rug, stared at her aunt's hand. Then she curled her own fingers, all of them, at the cat. It walked away. She beckoned at the fan, at the door, at a pigeon on the window ledge.
Yamini laughed and curled her fingers at Manjula. "Come, come." Manjula toddled straight into her arms.

qa.q: What did Manjula beckon at after the cat walked away?
qa.a: At the fan, the door and a pigeon on the window ledge.

qa.q: What was Manjula likely feeling as she beckoned at everything?
qa.a: She was curious and excited to try the new gesture, without fully knowing what it did; walking into Yamini's arms shows delight when it finally worked.

qa.q: How did Yamini help Manjula learn what the gesture means?
qa.a: She beckoned to Manjula herself, so Manjula felt what "come" means by walking into her arms.

qa.q: What would change if Yamini had laughed at her and turned away?
qa.a: Manjula would not get a clear response, so the beckoning might stay a meaningless copy for longer.

grounding: A toddler copies an adult's beckoning gesture without full understanding, and its meaning follows the response she gets.

"Kunal, did you see? He gave the thumbs-up when the milk spilled!"
"He doesn't know what it means yet," said Kunal. "He's copying me."
Rafiq, sticky with milk, held his thumb up again and grinned.
"So what do we do?"
"Show him. Thumbs-up when he finishes the puzzle. Not now."
Later Rafiq pressed the last puzzle piece in. Kunal's thumb went up. "Yes!" Rafiq looked at Kunal's hand, then lifted his own thumb.

qa.q: When did Rafiq first give the thumbs-up in this scene?
qa.a: When the milk spilled.

qa.q: What might Rafiq have been feeling when he held his thumb up after the spill?
qa.a: He was probably just playful and pleased with the gesture, copying Kunal without understanding it; after the puzzle he seemed proud and connected.

qa.q: What small step did Kunal suggest to give the gesture meaning?
qa.a: Using the thumbs-up only at real achievements, like finishing the puzzle, so Rafiq links it with success.

qa.q: Why might the other adult react differently to the spilled-milk thumbs-up?
qa.a: They may find it funny or odd, while Kunal knows Rafiq is just copying him.

grounding: A toddler copies a thumbs-up without understanding, and an adult gives it meaning through the response.

subtype: Beckoning and thumbs-up copied from adults [Expressing]
passage:
Crèche note, Thursday. From Swati.
Preeti has started copying grown-up gestures. She curls her fingers to say “come here” to the other children, the way her father does at pickup.
Today she dropped her cup of water, looked at me, and gave a big thumbs-up.
I didn't laugh or say “good.” I said, “Uh-oh, water fell. Let's get a cloth.” She watched my face and helped wipe.
She's copying the shapes; the meaning comes from how we answer.

qa.q: What did Preeti give Swati after dropping her cup?
qa.a: She gave a big thumbs-up.

qa.q: What was Preeti likely feeling when she gave a thumbs-up after the spill?
qa.a: She was probably curious and a bit unsure, trying out a gesture she had copied and watching to see what it meant, rather than being pleased about the spill.

qa.q: Why was Swati's response a good one?
qa.a: Swati named what really happened and did not praise the thumbs-up, so Preeti can learn what the gesture means from the response.

qa.q: What would change if Swati had laughed and said "good"?
qa.a: Preeti might learn that a thumbs-up goes with spilling things, giving the gesture the wrong meaning.

grounding: It shows a toddler copying come-here and thumbs-up gestures without full understanding, with meaning following the adult's response.
